title: Data Analysis with Python and pandas
subtitle: Load, clean, explore, combine and chart real-world data in Jupyter notebooks with pandas and matplotlib, and turn what you find into a clear, honest story.
outcomes: Work in Jupyter notebooks, in PyCharm or JupyterLab, and keep an analysis reproducible
Load CSV data with pandas and check its size, types and gaps before trusting it
Clean data: missing values, numbers stored as text, dates, duplicates and inconsistent labels
Select, filter, group, reshape and merge data to answer questions
Make clear charts with matplotlib and tell an honest story with the evidence and its caveats
prerequisites: Basic Python: variables, lists, dictionaries, loops and functions (the Python Programming with PyCharm course covers them). You need Python 3 and PyCharm (the free version is enough); the course installs pandas, matplotlib and JupyterLab, and every dataset comes with the labs.
description:
Most of a data analyst's time goes on getting data into shape and asking it the right questions. In this course you do both with pandas, Python's most widely used library for tables of data, working in Jupyter notebooks: in PyCharm, if your edition supports them, or in JupyterLab. You'll follow one fictional football season from a messy CSV file to a finished story: load the results and take stock, then clean them, removing duplicate rows, fixing team names typed five different ways, converting attendances stored as text and deciding what to do about a postponed match.

Next you'll select and filter matches, group and aggregate them, reshape each match into one row per team, and merge in each club's stadium details, building the league table from scratch. Finally you'll chart the title race with matplotlib, choose the right chart for each question, and write up what the season shows, and what it can't. Every module ends with a lab whose results you can check exactly, and the course ends with a project on a new dataset: a weekend food market's sales and the weather.

modules.title: Notebooks and loading data
modules.summary: Set up a Jupyter notebook in PyCharm or JupyterLab, meet pandas' DataFrames and Series, and load a season of football results to see what's in it, and what's wrong with it.

lessons.title: Notebooks for data analysis
objectives: Explain what a Jupyter notebook is and why analysts use one
Create and run a notebook in PyCharm or JupyterLab
key_points: A Jupyter notebook (an .ipynb file) mixes code cells, their output and text cells written in Markdown, so an analysis and its explanation live in one document.
Code runs in a kernel, a Python process that keeps variables between cells; cells can be run in any order, so restart the kernel and run all cells before you trust or share a result.
The value of a cell's last line is displayed automatically, which is how a DataFrame appears as a table without print().

Whether PyCharm can create and run notebooks depends on its edition and version, so check JetBrains' documentation for yours; JupyterLab (pip install jupyterlab, then jupyter lab) runs them in a browser.
Keep the notebooks, the data files and the virtual environment in one project folder, so a notebook can open the files by name.

lessons.title: DataFrames and Series
objectives: Describe how a DataFrame is made of columns, called Series, that share an index
Create a DataFrame, pick out columns and calculate with them
key_points: A pandas DataFrame is a table: named columns, each holding one type of data, and an index that labels the rows (0, 1, 2 and so on unless you choose otherwise).
Each column is a Series: df['home_goals'] selects one, and df[['home_team', 'away_team']], with a list inside the brackets, selects several as a new DataFrame.
Operations work on whole columns at once: df['home_goals'] + df['away_goals'] adds every row's values without a loop.
Every column has a dtype: int64 for whole numbers, float64 for decimals, bool, datetime64 for dates and times, and text, shown as object in pandas 2 and as str in pandas 3.
Missing values show as NaN (NaT for dates); a column of whole numbers with a gap becomes float64 unless you use the nullable Int64 type.

lessons.title: Loading a CSV and taking a first look
objectives: Load a CSV file with read_csv and check what came in
List a dataset's problems before analysing it
key_points: pd.read_csv('matches.csv') reads a comma-separated file into a DataFrame, taking column names from the first line; options such as parse_dates, thousands=',' and na_values handle dates, number formats and missing markers.
First checks: df.shape for the number of rows and columns, df.head() for the first rows, df.info() for each column's type and non-missing count, and df.describe() for numeric summaries.
df.isna().sum() counts missing values per column; pandas reads empty cells and common markers such as NA and n/a as missing, but not a dash or the word unknown.
A number column read as text, such as attendance written as 15,957, signals a formatting problem: describe() leaves it out, and it can't be summed until it's converted.
Counting each distinct value with value_counts() exposes inconsistent labels, such as a lower-case name or one with a space at the end.

modules.title: Cleaning data
modules.summary: Fix the problems real data arrives with: missing values, numbers stored as text, dates, duplicates and inconsistent labels, then save a clean copy you can trust.

lessons.title: Missing values
objectives: Find missing values and work out what each one means
Drop, fill or keep missing values for a good reason
key_points: Before fixing a gap, ask why it's there: a postponed match has no score because it wasn't played, so filling it with 0-0 would invent a result.
dropna() removes rows with missing values (subset=['home_goals'] limits which columns it checks) and fillna(value) fills them; both return a new DataFrame, so assign the result.
Summaries such as mean() and sum() skip missing values by default, so an average attendance uses only the matches where a crowd was recorded.
A boolean mask such as df['home_goals'].isna() picks out the rows with gaps, so you can look at them before deciding what to do.
Keep a log of every cleaning decision, such as removing one postponed match, because each one changes what your results mean.

lessons.title: Fixing types: numbers, dates and text
objectives: Convert text to numbers and dates without losing values
Clean text columns with pandas' string methods
key_points: pd.to_numeric() converts text to numbers; errors='coerce' turns anything it can't read into NaN, which silently loses values such as 15,957 unless the commas are removed first with .str.replace(',', '').
pd.to_datetime() turns date text into datetimes, which sort in time order and give parts such as .dt.month and .dt.day_name(); for day-first dates such as 07/06/2025, pass dayfirst=True or a format.
String methods under .str work on a whole column: .str.strip() removes spaces at the ends, .str.title() capitalises each word and .str.contains() finds text.
astype() changes a column's type: astype(int) once a goals column has no gaps, or astype('Int64') for whole numbers that may have gaps.
Check every conversion by counting missing values before and after: a conversion that creates new gaps has probably misread something.

Assign changes with df[col] = ... or df.loc[rows, col] = ...; chained assignment such as df[df.x > 1]['y'] = 0 doesn't reliably change df, and in pandas 3 it never does.

modules.title: Selecting, grouping and merging
modules.summary: Ask questions of your data: pick out rows and columns, filter with conditions, group and aggregate, reshape, and merge tables, building a league table from the raw results.

lessons.title: Selecting and filtering rows and columns
objectives: Select rows and columns by label, position and condition
Combine conditions to answer specific questions
key_points: df.loc[rows, columns] selects by label or condition, as in df.loc[df['home_team'] == 'Riverside Rovers', ['date', 'attendance']]; df.iloc[rows, columns] selects by position, as in df.iloc[:5, :3].
A comparison such as df['home_goals'] > df['away_goals'] gives a Series of True and False, called a boolean mask, and df[mask] keeps the rows where it's True.
Combine conditions with & (and), | (or) and ~ (not), each condition in its own brackets: df[(df['home_goals'] == 0) & (df['away_goals'] == 0)].
df.query('home_goals == 0 and away_goals == 0') writes the same filter as readable text, and isin(['Harbour City', 'Lakeside Town']) tests whether values are in a list.
sort_values('attendance', ascending=False) orders the rows, and head(n) or nlargest(n, 'attendance') picks the top ones.

lessons.title: Grouping and aggregating
objectives: Summarise data by group with groupby and agg
Count values and proportions, and make a grid with pivot_table
key_points: groupby splits rows into groups, applies a calculation to each and combines the results: df.groupby('home_team')['attendance'].mean() is each team's average home crowd.
agg() computes several summaries at once, each named, as in agg(P=('points', 'size'), Pts=('points', 'sum')).
value_counts() counts each distinct value, and normalize=True gives proportions: in this season home teams won 41.4% of matches, away teams 37.9%, and 20.7% were drawn.
Summing a column of True and False counts the Trues, which is a quick way to count wins.
pivot_table() makes a grid from long data, such as points by team and matchday, with aggfunc='sum' and fill_value=0 for empty cells.

lessons.title: Reshaping and merging tables
objectives: Reshape match data into one row per team per match
Merge two tables on a key and check the result
key_points: A league table needs one row per team per match, so each match becomes two rows: one from the home team's side and one from the away team's.
rename(columns={...}) renames columns, assign(venue='home') adds one, and pd.concat([home, away], ignore_index=True) stacks DataFrames that have the same columns.
merge() joins two DataFrames on matching key columns: left_on='home_team', right_on='team' links each match to its home ground's details.
how= decides which rows survive a merge: 'inner' keeps rows found in both tables, 'left' keeps every row of the left table and fills the gaps with NaN, and 'outer' keeps everything.
After a merge, check the number of rows and look for NaN in the new columns, because a misspelt key fails to match without any error.

setup: Your data-analysis project with pandas installed

steps.do: Group by team to make the table: P, W, D, L, GF, GA, GD and Pts, sorted by points, then goal difference, then goals scored.

table = long.groupby("team").agg(

modules.title: Charts and stories
modules.summary: Turn findings into clear charts with matplotlib, choose the right chart for each question, and tell an honest story with data: a headline, the evidence and the caveats.

lessons.title: Charts with matplotlib
objectives: Draw line, bar and other charts with matplotlib's figure and axes
Label and save a chart so it can be shared
key_points: fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates a figure (the whole image) and axes (one chart); methods on ax draw it: ax.plot for lines, ax.bar and ax.barh for bars, ax.hist for histograms and ax.scatter for points.
Label everything: ax.set_title(), ax.set_xlabel() and ax.set_ylabel(), and ax.legend() when a chart has more than one series.
fig.savefig('points.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight') saves the chart as an image to share; in a notebook the chart also appears under its cell.
pandas can draw straight from a DataFrame, as in table['Pts'].plot.barh(); it uses matplotlib underneath and returns the axes for further labelling.
In a .py script rather than a notebook, plt.show() displays the figures, and savefig works the same either way.

steps.code:

cumulative = by_round.cumsum()
cumulative[["Hilltop United", "Riverside Rovers"]].T

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
for team in ["Hilltop United", "Riverside Rovers", "Northgate Athletic"]:
    ax.plot(cumulative.index, cumulative[team], marker="o", label=team)
ax.set_title("Hilltop United caught Riverside Rovers on the last day")
ax.set_xlabel("Matchday")

ax.legend()

lessons.title: Choosing the right chart
objectives: Match a chart type to the question it answers
Avoid design choices that mislead
key_points: Match the chart to the question: bars compare amounts across categories, lines show change over time, histograms show how values are spread, and scatter plots show how two numbers relate.
Start a bar chart's axis at zero, because readers judge bars by their length; a cut-off axis makes small differences look big.
Sort bars by value, and use horizontal bars when the labels are long, such as team names.
Use colour to make one thing stand out rather than to decorate, and keep the number of lines or colours small.
Avoid 3-D effects and pie charts with many slices: both make values hard to compare.

walkthrough.title: A bar chart that reads at a glance

steps.code:
points = long.groupby("team")["points"].sum().sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
bars = ax.barh(points.index, points.values, color="lightgrey")
ax.set_xlim(0, None)
ax.set_title("Final points")
ax.set_xlabel("Points")

lessons.title: Telling a story with data
objectives: Structure a finding as a headline, evidence and caveats
Keep an analysis reproducible from the first cell to the last
key_points: A data story answers a question: a headline that states the answer, the evidence that supports it, and the caveats that limit it.
Give charts titles that state the finding, such as 'Hilltop United caught Riverside Rovers on the last day', rather than labels such as 'Points by matchday'.
Put numbers in context: 12 home wins against 11 away wins in 29 matches is too small a difference, in too few matches, to show a home advantage.
Say what the data can't show: this season has only 29 played matches, one postponed match and two attendances missing.

project.title: Analyse a weekend food market
project.brief: A fictional weekend food market has sent you two files. sales.csv records, for 16 market days in June and July 2025, how many of each product each of its five stalls sold and at what price; weather.csv gives each day's weather and top temperature. The market's organisers want to know which stalls and products earn the most, whether Sundays differ from Saturdays, and how the weather affects sales, especially the ice cream stall's. Clean the data (it has duplicate rows, a few missing figures, product names typed inconsistently and dates written day first), merge the two files, answer the questions with groupby and charts, and write a one-page story with recommendations for the organisers. Keep a cleaning log, and be honest about what 16 days of data can and can't show.
deliverables: A notebook that runs from top to bottom after restarting the kernel
A cleaning log: every problem found, what was done and why
Revenue (units sold x unit price) by stall and by product, with the top earners named
A comparison of Saturdays with Sundays, and of sunny, cloudy and rainy days, after merging in the weather
At least three charts, each saved as an image, with titles that state their findings
A one-page story with a headline, evidence, caveats and two or three recommendations

rubric.name: Story and recommendations
rubric.description: A clear headline, evidence with numbers, honest caveats about 16 days of data, and recommendations that follow from the evidence.
